steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing COPR, a method for continually learning human preferences in LLMs via optimal policy regularization. Motivate continual alignment, describe the method and the new benchmarks, and list the contributions.

steps.text:

- RLHF and why it does not support continual learning
- COPR: the proposed approach
- First study of CL for alignment; new TIL and DIL benchmarks
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are vital tools in natural language processing (NLP), and they could bridge human language and machine understanding. Learning human preferences is a crucial step so that language models generate responses that are useful to users and also follow ethical and societal norms, in other words helpful and harmless responses. But LLMs have a fundamental challenge in aligning with human preferences and values, and this hinders their full potential.

The traditional alignment method is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which involves supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward model (RM) training, and policy model training. This pipeline is complex and it is not flexible for continual learning (CL) of human preferences, so existing work often has to retrain the models to adapt to dynamic preferences, and this needs huge computation resources. So there is a pressing need to research continual alignment methods that address this limitation, so that LLMs can better follow evolving human preferences and values while still generating helpful responses.

- COPR = Continually learning human preference through Optimal Policy Regularization
  - Figure 1(a): sequence of optimal policy distributions as preferences evolve; used as supervision + regularization to finetune policy
  - close to optimal policy on current task, not far from historical optimal policies
  - function regularization in CL taxonomy; scoring module (like RM) gives preference order, learns unlabeled data
- first to study CL of alignment; first TIL + DIL benchmarks (Section 4.1)
  - TIL: HH, Reddit TL;DR (CarperAI), enhanced IMDB from RL4LMs; DIL: SHP, 18 domains
- Contributions: COPR (simple, RL-free); TIL + DIL benchmarks; outperforms CL and alignment methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) are vital tools in natural language processing (NLP), and they could bridge human language and machine understanding. Learning human preferences is a crucial step so that language models generate responses that are useful to users and also follow ethical and societal norms, in other words helpful and harmless responses. But LLMs have a fundamental challenge in aligning with human preferences and values, and this hinders their full potential.

The traditional alignment method is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which involves supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward model (RM) training, and policy model training. This pipeline is complex and it is not flexible for continual learning (CL) of human preferences, so existing work often has to retrain the models to adapt to dynamic preferences, and this needs huge computation resources. So there is a pressing need to research continual alignment methods that address this limitation, so that LLMs can better follow evolving human preferences and values while still generating helpful responses.

In this paper we propose a new approach called COPR, Continually learning human preference through Optimal Policy Regularization. As shown in Figure 1(a), our method computes the sequence of optimal policy distributions in scenarios where the human preferences evolve continuously. Then we use these optimal policy distributions as a supervision signal and a regularization objective to finetune the policy model. Intuitively, COPR makes the policy distribution close to the optimal policy on the current task and it also prevents it from deviating too far from the historically optimal policies of past tasks. In the state-of-the-art continual learning taxonomy, our method is in the category of function regularization. We also maintain a scoring module, inspired by the reward model in the RLHF pipeline, which gives the preference order for responses and can learn unlabeled data.

As far as we know, we are the first to study CL of alignment methods. To evaluate fairly, we construct the first Task Incremental Learning (TIL) and Domain Incremental Learning (DIL) benchmarks for continual learning of human preferences, based on existing human preference datasets (Section 4.1). The TIL benchmark uses the Helpful and Harmless preference (HH) data, the Reddit TL;DR summary human preference data provided by CarperAI, and the enhanced IMDB Sentiment Text Generation benchmark released by RL4LMs. The DIL benchmark uses the Standard Human Preference (SHP) data, which has 18 domains like academia, baking, physics, etc.

Our main contributions are:

- We propose COPR, which is a simple RL-free algorithm to continually learn human preferences.

- We introduce the first TIL and DIL benchmarks for continual value alignment.

- Our experiments show COPR outperforms existing CL and alignment methods on the TIL and DIL benchmarks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the realm of natural language processing (NLP), large language models (LLMs) are vital tools that have the potential to bridge human language and machine understanding. Learning human preferences is a crucial step towards ensuring that language models generate responses that are not only useful to users but also adhere to ethical and societal norms, namely helpful and harmless responses [1]. However, LLMs face a fundamental challenge in aligning with human preferences and values, which hinders their full potential.

Traditional alignment methods, namely Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [2,3], involve supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward model (RM) training, and policy model training. This complex pipeline lacks flexibility for continual learning (CL) of human preferences, so existing work [1] often has to retrain models to adapt to dynamic preferences, which requires huge computation resources. Hence, there is a pressing need for research into continual alignment methods that address this limitation, enabling LLMs to better adhere to evolving human preferences and values while generating helpful responses.

In this paper, we propose an innovative approach to Continually learning human preference through Optimal Policy Regularization (COPR). Our method, as depicted in Figure 1(a), computes the sequence of optimal policy distributions in scenarios where human preferences evolve continuously. We then use the optimal policy distributions as a supervision signal and regularization objective to finetune the policy model. Intuitively, COPR makes the distribution of the policy close to the optimal policy on the current task and prevents it from deviating too far from the historically optimal policies of past tasks. According to the state-of-the-art continual learning taxonomy [4], our method belongs to the category of function regularization. Inspired by the reward model in the RLHF pipeline, we maintain a scoring module that gives the preference order for responses and can learn unlabeled data.

To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study the CL of alignment methods. For fair evaluation, we construct the first Task Incremental Learning (TIL) and Domain Incremental Learning (DIL) benchmarks for continual learning of human preferences, based on existing human preference datasets (Section 4.1). The TIL benchmark uses Helpful and Harmless preference (HH) [1] data, Reddit TL;DR summary [2] human preference data provided by CarperAI, and the enhanced IMDB [5] Sentiment Text Generation benchmark released by RL4LMs [6]. The DIL benchmark uses the Standard Human Preference (SHP) [7] data, which has 18 domains including academia, baking, physics, etc.

In summary, our main contributions are:

- We propose COPR, a simple RL-free algorithm for continually learning human preferences.

- We introduce the first TIL and DIL benchmarks for continual value alignment.

- Our experiments show that COPR outperforms existing CL and alignment methods on the TIL and DIL benchmarks.
